cards.explanation: The answer is False. The Benjamites, the tribe of Benjamin, failed to drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. The Jebusites were a people already living in the city. The writer adds, “So to this day the Jebusites live there among the Benjamites.”

The answer is True. The house of Joseph, Joseph's descendants, attack Bethel, and the verse says it plainly: “…and the LORD was with them.” (Judges 1:22) That's a good place to be when you march on a city, friends. I'd take that over a head start every time.

The answer is spies, friends. Judges 1:23 says they sent spies to Bethel, which used to be called Luz. Spies are the folks you send before an attack. And the very next verse has those spies spotting a man coming out of the city.

The answer is how to get into the city, bakers. The spies say to the man, “Please show us how to get into the city, and we will treat you kindly.” (Judges 1:24) They ask for the way in and nothing else. Short and polite, like asking a neighbor for directions.

The answer is that they promise to treat him kindly, friends. The spies tell him, “…and we will treat you kindly.” (Judges 1:24) And verse 25 says that after they put the city to the sword, they released that man and all his family. That's the promise on the table, and it's the one they're said to keep.

The answer is True, bakers. Judges 1:25 says they put the city to the sword “…but released that man and all his family.” He showed them the entrance, and he and his family were released. That's the kindness the spies promised back in verse 24.

The answer is city, friends. The man went to the land of the Hittites, a people living in that region, “…built a city, and called it Luz…” (Judges 1:26) He didn't just walk off. He built something new.

The answer is that they were determined to dwell there, bakers. The text says, “for the Canaanites were determined to dwell in that land.” (Judges 1:27) Those five towns weren't going to empty out on their own. These people had made up their minds to stay.

The answer is that they press them into forced labor, friends. “When Israel became stronger, they pressed the Canaanites into forced labor, but they never drove them out completely.” (Judges 1:28) Israel got stronger and put the Canaanites to work. Then comes that little “but,” and it carries the whole verse. It's like me saying I'll clean out the junk drawer and then closing it with half the stuff still inside.

The answer is False, bakers. The Amorites, one of the peoples of the land, forced the Danites into the hill country. They “…did not allow them to come down into the plain.” (Judges 1:34) The tribe of Dan was the one getting pushed around.

The answer is False, friends. Judges 1:35 says, “But when the house of Joseph grew in strength, they pressed the Amorites into forced labor.” The house of Joseph got stronger and the Amorites got put to work, but the verse never says they were driven out. That's like shoving the dough to the other side of the counter and calling the counter clean.

The answer is True, bakers. The angel of the LORD says that God brought Israel up out of Egypt and led them into the land He promised to their fathers. He also says God said He would never break His covenant with them. (Judges 2:1) A covenant is a binding promise, and this one isn't going anywhere.

The answer is to tear them down, friends. The angel says Israel was not to make a covenant with the people of this land, but to tear down their altars. (Judges 2:2) Altars to other gods weren't supposed to stay standing in the land God gave them.

The answer is that the people of the land will not be driven out, bakers. The angel says, “So now I tell you that I will not drive out these people before you…” (Judges 2:3) That comes right after “Yet you have not obeyed My voice.” (Judges 2:2) The people who were supposed to leave will stay.

The answer is True, friends. The angel says the people of the land “…will be thorns in your sides…” (Judges 2:3) A thorn in your side is something that keeps bothering you. Nobody wants one, and that's the word the angel picks.
The answer is snare, bakers. The angel says, “…and their gods will be a snare to you.” (Judges 2:3) A snare is a trap. Think of a trap sitting where you walk every day.

The answer is weep, friends. “When the angel of the LORD had spoken these words to all the Israelites, the people lifted up their voices and wept.” (Judges 2:4) I think this one hurts. The words they just heard were heavy, and the whole crowd cried out.

The answer is that they offer sacrifices to the LORD, bakers. Judges 2:5 says, “So they called that place Bochim and offered sacrifices there to the LORD.” After the weeping, they brought sacrifices to the LORD at that very spot.
